title: Realizing Error Suppression in Partially Fault-Tolerant Quantum Simulations with IBM Quantum Computers
authors: Henry Froland, Dorota M. Grabowska, Sebastian Grieninger, Jeremy Hartse, Anne L. Lashbrook, Zhiyao Li, Ziyuan Li, Sarah J. M. Powell, Martin J. Savage, Xiaojun Yao, Nikita A. Zemlevskiy
abstract: Quantum error-detecting codes offer a near-term path for improving the performance of quantum simulations on noisy hardware. Using IBM's superconducting quantum computer ibm_boston, we show that partially fault-tolerant encoded quantum simulations of the Ising model in 1+1D and 2+1D outperform their unencoded counterparts in estimating local observables. To represent 42 logical qubits on the heavy-hex quantum processor, 21 blocks of the [[4, 2, 2]] Iceberg code and up to 136 physical qubits are used. By pairing fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations, this scheme preserves many of the benefits of error detection while avoiding the overhead typically required for a fully fault-tolerant logical gate set. The encoding's square logical connectivity, together with the freedom to place logical qubits within each block, enables simulations of a 2D spatial lattice with lower circuit depth than the unencoded implementation requires. We introduce Observable-Ranked Postselection, a selective-filtering technique based on syndrome correlations that recovers reliable results without the prohibitive shot loss of full syndrome postselection. Under the cumulative effect of device errors, this encoding improves local-observable accuracy over the unencoded baseline by 2-6% at intermediate times in 1+1D simulations, growing with circuit depth to over 200% in 2+1D at the latest times studied.
summary: This paper demonstrates how partially fault-tolerant quantum encoding can significantly boost the accuracy of quantum simulations on current noisy hardware. By using the [[4, 2, 2]] code and an advanced filtering technique called ORP, the authors show substantial improvements in estimating local observables for the Ising model compared to unencoded runs. This work provides a practical roadmap for scaling complex quantum simulations beyond immediate NISQ limitations.
main_problem: The primary goal is to improve quantum simulation performance on noisy, near-term hardware by implementing error suppression techniques.
main_result: Partially fault-tolerant encoding significantly outperforms unencoded simulations, showing accuracy improvements of 2-6% in 1+1D and over 200% in 2+1D at late times studied.
method: The authors use a partially fault-tolerant scheme combining syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations, alongside Observable-Ranked Postselection (ORP) for data filtering.
model_or_system: Simulations focus on the Ising model in 1+1D and 2+1D lattices. The physical implementation uses IBM's superconducting quantum computer (`ibm boston`) with a heavy-hex processor, employing the [[4, 2, 2]] Iceberg code.
key_observables: Local observables are estimated; key diagnostics include the logical error rate and the improvement factor in local-observable accuracy.
important_parameters: The comparison is made between unencoded vs. partially fault-tolerant regimes, showing performance gains that scale with circuit depth (especially in 2+1D).
main_assumptions: The approach balances error rate improvements from FT against overhead by using a pFT scheme; ORP assumes the optimal cutoff level balances bias reduction against statistical uncertainty inflation.
figures_summary: Figure 1a details the structure and stabilizers of the [[4, 2, 2]] code block. Figure 1b shows the placement of these blocks on the ibm boston processor. Figure 1c illustrates the circuit operations involving syndrome extraction and non-FT logical gates.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the need for error suppression in quantum simulations, details the use of the [[4, 2, 2]] code block structure, explains the partially fault-tolerant protocol combining FT syndrome measurement with nFT logic, and finally presents results showing quantitative improvements over unencoded baselines using ORP.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the critical gap between NISQ devices and fault-tolerance by proposing a resource-efficient, intermediate error correction strategy applicable to simulating condensed matter models like the Ising model.

Figure 4 shows the percentage improvement in α over time for R = 1 in 1D and 2D simulations. The im- provement in the results from runs with encoding grows approximately linearly in 2D, with an average slope of 23.5 ± 0.8% in the melting regime and 22.8 ± 0.5% in the localized regime. Because each caught error prevents corruption over a lightcone volume scaling as O(t2) in 2D compared to O(t) in 1D, detection has greater leverage in 2D and the encoding improvement grows with t. The greater than 200% improvement in 2D is also driven by rapidly decohering unencoded results, as is similarly seen in Fig. 3b).
